bibliography.abstract: Time geography, introduced by Torsten Hägerstrand in 1970, has evolved from a framework for studying constraints on daily activity into a shared vocabulary adopted across diverse research domains. How the literature that grew from Hägerstrand’s work diffused, and whether its core concepts held up as it expanded, have not been examined as a whole. We address this gap through a scientometric study of 13,371 English-language journal articles from 1970 to 2024 assembled from OpenAlex and Scopus through a seed-and-expand procedure that combines keyword searches with citation tracking. Changepoint detection divides the period into four stages. Keyword and co-occurrence analysis tracks which themes endured and how they were used. A citation network shows how the literature diffused across fields, and a co-authorship community network shows how its most prolific authors collaborate. Publication grew from a North America-Europe concentration into a polycentric network spanning Asia, North America, and Europe, and from human geography journals into transportation, GIS, and urban journals. Time geography, mobility, gender, and place remained among the most frequent keywords in every stage, accessibility and activity space rose to lead the most recent stage, and the pairing of these terms with GIS held while their leading co-occurring keywords shifted toward transit equity and tracking data. The literature has separated into ten bodies of work, each in a different applied field and four of them concerned with human activity in cities, which draw on the same concepts but cite mainly within their own field. Its most prolific authors work in eight distinct communities linked through a few authors. Time geography has thus spread by gaining new fields and data sources rather than by replacing what it began with.
bibliography.title: Evolution and diffusion of time geography from 1970 to 2024

en.caveats: The dataset is restricted to English-language journal articles indexed in OpenAlex and Scopus, which may omit non-English contributions or book-length treatises central to the discipline's early history.
en.what: This scientometric study analyzed 13,371 journal articles from 1970 to 2024 to map the intellectual growth and cross-disciplinary spread of time geography. Using network analysis and changepoint detection, it shows the field evolved across four distinct stages, expanding from its origins in human geography into transportation, GIS, and urban studies while shifting geographically from North America and Europe to include Asia. The literature has fragmented into ten distinct clusters—four focused on urban human activity—where authors draw on core concepts like activity spaces and transit equity but predominantly cite within their specific subfields.
en.why: It documents how time geography grew by absorbing new tracking data sources and applied domains rather than abandoning its foundational concepts, though its literature now operates in siloed disciplinary clusters.
